opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. If I had to pick the papers that really changed the trajectory, I'd group them into a few waves.

The first is the deep learning breakthrough itself: AlexNet in 2012. The architecture wasn't totally new, but it showed that with enough data, GPUs, and some practical tricks like ReLU and dropout, neural networks could crush hand-engineered approaches. That shifted the whole field's mindset. ResNet a few years later mattered just as much in a quieter way. Residual connections made very deep networks trainable, and that idea is still inside basically every large model today.

The second wave is the Transformer, "Attention Is All You Need" in 2017. What made it so influential wasn't only that attention worked well for translation. It was a simple, highly parallelizable architecture that scaled beautifully on modern hardware. Almost everything since, including language, vision, speech, and even protein models, has been built on that foundation.

Third, I'd point to the pretraining paradigm: GPT, BERT, and then GPT-2 and GPT-3. BERT showed that self-supervised pretraining followed by fine-tuning could dominate benchmarks. The GPT line pushed the more radical idea that a single generative model, trained just to predict the next token, could pick up surprisingly general abilities. GPT-3's in-context learning was a real "wait, what?" moment for a lot of researchers.

Closely tied to that are the scaling laws papers, first from OpenAI and then DeepMind's Chinchilla work. They turned progress into something closer to engineering: if you put in this much compute and data, you can roughly predict the loss you'll get. That gave organizations the confidence to make enormous bets, and I think that predictability is underrated as a driver of the last few years.

Then there's alignment and post-training: RLHF, especially InstructGPT. Raw pretrained models are powerful but awkward to use. Learning from human preferences is what turned them into assistants people actually want to talk to. A lot of what made ChatGPT feel like a leap came from that layer rather than from raw capability.

More recently, I'd highlight work on reasoning, from chain-of-thought prompting to using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on math and code. It suggests a new scaling axis: instead of only scaling pretraining, you can scale the compute a model spends thinking at inference time, and train it to use that thinking well.

I'd also give credit to things that aren't flashy papers: ImageNet as a dataset and benchmark, open-source frameworks like PyTorch, and systems work on distributed training and efficient attention. Progress in AI has always been a mix of ideas, data, and infrastructure. The papers we remember tend to be the ones where all three came together at the right moment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses several influential AI papers and methods but does not mention Mamba or identify it as an intellectual precursor to Kimi’s KDA.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, so let me try to pick out a few threads rather than give you a list of a hundred papers.

If I had to name the single most consequential paper of the last decade, it's "Attention Is All You Need" from 2017. The Transformer did something subtle: it didn't just introduce a better architecture, it introduced an architecture that scales cleanly with compute and data. Before that, with recurrent networks, you couldn't parallelize training across sequence length, and that was a practical ceiling. The Transformer removed that ceiling, and almost everything since has been built on top of it.

But I'd argue the Transformer alone isn't the whole story. The second thread is the scaling laws work, first from OpenAI in 2020 and then the Chinchilla paper from DeepMind in 2022. Those papers changed how people think. They turned model building from an art into something closer to engineering. You could predict, with real confidence, what you'd get if you spent ten times more compute. That predictability is what justified the enormous investments that followed. Chinchilla in particular corrected a mistake the whole field was making, which was training models that were too large on too little data.

The third thread is pretraining itself as a paradigm. GPT-1 and BERT in 2018 showed that you could learn general representations from unlabeled text and then adapt them. GPT-3 in 2020 showed that if you push that far enough, you get in-context learning, where the model does new tasks without any gradient updates at all. I remember reading that paper and feeling the ground shift a little. It wasn't that it was clever. It was that the capability emerged without anyone designing it.

Then you have the alignment side. The InstructGPT paper and reinforcement learning from human feedback are, I think, underrated by people outside the field. A raw pretrained model is strange and hard to use. RLHF is what turned it into something ordinary people could talk to, and that is really what made ChatGPT a product rather than a research demo.

Going further back, I'd mention AlexNet in 2012, because it's the moment deep learning stopped being a fringe belief and became the default. And I'd mention the ResNet paper, because residual connections quietly solved the problem of training very deep networks, and they're still inside every Transformer today.

More recently, the thing I find most interesting is the shift toward reasoning, with chain-of-thought prompting and then models trained with reinforcement learning to think for longer before answering. That's a different axis of scaling, test-time compute rather than training compute, and I think we're still early in understanding it.

If there's a common lesson across all of these, it's that the most influential ideas tend to be simple ones that remove a bottleneck to scale, rather than clever ones that add complexity. That's the pattern I keep seeing.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Mamba or Kimi’s KDA, or describe Mamba as an intellectual precursor to KDA.

astra-6.text:
I’d highlight a few lines of work. Backpropagation gave us a practical way to train multilayer neural networks. Later, systems like AlexNet showed how much progress you could get by combining those networks with large datasets and GPU computing.

For today’s language models, “Attention Is All You Need” was a major turning point. The Transformer made it easier to train on sequences at scale. Combined with self-supervised learning—learning from the structure of data rather than requiring a human label for every example—it helped make large-scale pretraining possible.

I’d also point to reinforcement learning, especially the work behind AlphaGo and AlphaZero, which combined learning with search. And more recently, instruction tuning and learning from human feedback have helped turn capable language models into systems people can interact with more usefully.

What stands out to me is that progress rarely comes from a paper alone. It comes when a good method meets enough data, computing power, and a reliable way to test whether it actually works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses backpropagation, AlexNet, Transformers, self-supervised learning, reinforcement learning, instruction tuning, and human feedback, but does not identify Mamba as a precursor to Kimi’s KDA.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d point to a few connected lines of work. Backpropagation gave us a practical way to train multilayer neural networks. Convolutional networks, and later AlexNet, showed how much progress could come from combining the right architecture with large datasets and enough computing power.

For today’s language models, “Attention Is All You Need” is a major milestone. The Transformer made it easier to train at scale and capture relationships across a sequence. But the training methods matter just as much: self-supervised learning lets models learn from enormous amounts of unlabeled data, and instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback help turn that capability into something people can use.

I’d also highlight reinforcement learning, particularly the work behind AlphaGo, because it showed the power of combining learning with search. My view is that progress rarely comes from one paper alone. It comes when an architectural idea, a training method, data, and computing resources come together.
